idiom_name: function* typed Generator<T, TReturn, TNext> / IterableIterator<T>
implementation_notes: TypeScript types the JavaScript laziness model rather than adding its own: a function* has type Generator<T, TReturn, TNext> and is assignable to both Iterable<T> and Iterator<T>, an object is iterable when it implements Symbol.iterator, and for...of compiles to the same protocol, so APIs can accept Iterable<T> and get lazy, typed consumption. The type system does not encode the traversal contract (single-use vs re-iterable, memoized or not), so document it; the eager array pipeline remains simpler when the data is small or indexed access is required.
pitfalls: Generator is an Iterator, so a callee that accepts Iterable<T> and iterates it twice compiles fine and silently yields nothing the second time (or re-runs the source for factory-based iterables).
Typed arrays and lazy iterables are structurally different: passing an Iterable where a T[] is expected fails to compile, but passing an iterator into a helper that spreads it consumes it.
Downlevel targets without native generators (ES5 emit) require regenerator at runtime, changing performance and sometimes breaking Symbol.iterator assumptions.

variants.name: IteratorObject<T> helper chains (ES2025 lib)
variants.idiom_name: IteratorObject<T> with map/filter/take/drop/toArray from the ES2025 lib
variants.implementation_notes: Recent TypeScript lib targets type the iterator helpers (IteratorObject<T> with map, filter, take, drop, flatMap, reduce, toArray) that JavaScript added to iterator instances, so a lazy chain over an iterator can be expressed declaratively and still evaluated element by element; the helpers return IteratorObject, which is both an iterator and iterable. They require the matching lib (esnext.iterator/ES2025) and a runtime that ships them; the generator-based variant is the portable choice, and eager array methods remain right for small data.
pitfalls: Iterator helpers are typed only when the lib includes them: without esnext.iterator/ES2025 the exact same code does not type-check, and older runtimes throw at the first helper call.
Helper chains wrap a single iterator, so the chain is single-use like the source; storing and re-consuming it yields an empty pass.
Helper callbacks run lazily and interleaved with consumption, so side effects happen in pull order rather than in a batch (unlike Array.prototype.map/filter).

variants.name: Typed async generators and for await (ES2018)
variants.implementation_notes: Typed async iterables bring the same model to awaited sources: async function* has type AsyncGenerator<T>, AsyncIterable<T> is accepted by for await...of, and each pulled element may await I/O, giving backpressure per element. Use it for streams, sockets and paged APIs where the type-level contract matters; a synchronous generator is cheaper when nothing awaits, and a queue/pub-sub abstraction is needed when multiple consumers share one source.
pitfalls: Abandoning a for await loop does not cancel the underlying work: the async generator must be returned/cancelled, otherwise fetches continue and unhandled rejections surface later.
Async generators are single-consumer; two concurrent loops over one AsyncIterable split the stream nondeterministically.
Type-level AsyncIterable says nothing about laziness or closing semantics: an implementation may buffer eagerly, so backpressure assumptions belong in the documented contract.
